newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU widens retaliation to U.S trade measures. [CORRECTED 22:07 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EU widens retaliation to U.S trade measures. [CORRECTED 22:07 GMT]

text.p: The European Commission has widened its proposed retaliation to recent U.S. trade legislation to cover the effects of the D'Amato Bill, which seeks to quash dealings with Iran (corrects from Iraq) and Libya.

A spokesman for the Commission -- the European Union's executive -- confirmed on Sunday that the D'Amato Bill had been added to a list of measures the EU was taking to fight the Helms-Burton Act, Washington's controversial anti-Cuba laws.

The move is sure to irritate Washington officials who had hoped a high-profile campaign by their envoy Stuart Eizenstat last month had put the transatlantic trade row on the back burner until after the November U.S. presidential elections.
The Commission spokesman said the D'Amato Bill was added as a "written procedure" on Friday to a list of measures being finalised for agreement by foreign ministers of the EU's 15 states.
A written procedure is a decision agreed unanimously by the 20 European commissioners without need for debate or discussion.
Originally, the EU retaliatory measures concerned only the Helms-Burton Act -- an amalgamation of decades of U.S. anti-Cuba policy.
But EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan is believed to have persuaded fellow commissioners that the D'Amato Bill -- which became law in July -- was even more harmful to European trade interests.
The bill seeks to prevent foreign companies from investing in oil and allied industries of Iran and Libya -- countries deemed sponsors of international terrorism by Washington.

The European Union, which relies on 20 percent of its oil imports (corrects from exports) from these countries, is determined to fight what it considers to be increasing extra-territorial laws emanating from Washington.
The D'Amato Bill differs from the Helms-Burton Act by applying state sanctions to foreign companies investing in Iran (corrects from Iraq) and Libya.

The Cuba laws, among other things, allow naturalised Americans to sue foreign companies or individuals deemed to have benefitted from investments in property confiscated from them by the Cuban government since the communist revolution of 1959.

In July EU foreign ministers gave the Commission a mandate to pursue four areas of retaliation. These would forbid EU nationals or companies from abiding by U.S. court rulings; allow companies or individuals to counter sue; bar U.S. citizens involved in litigation from the EU and compile a "watchlist" of U.S. companies threatening lawsuits.

It is difficult to see how those measures can be translated into effective weapons against the U.S. government -- as would have to be the case with the D'Amato Bill -- but an EU official said on Sunday that they were intended rather to give Washington an excuse not to invoke the law.

"If the EU has counter-laws in place in place, it will be easier for President (Bill) Clinton to justify postponing any action with the excuse that national security was threatened by a conflict of jurisdiction," the official said.

Clinton suspended the practical implications of the Helms-Burton Act until January to give envoy Eizenstat the opportunity to convince U.S. allies to join a new, concerted effort to bring democracy to Cuba. The D'Amato Bill, however, is already law.
Although Clinton is believed to be privately opposed to aspects of both laws, analysts have said that he had little choice but to pass them in case they became an election issue.
